nodes.name: Z_p-extension
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field, $p$ be a prime. {\rm(i)} An extension $K_\infty/K$ is called a $\BZ_p$-extension, if it is Galois with $\Gamma=\Gal(K_\infty/K)\cong\BZ_p$ as topological groups. {\rm(ii)} If $K_\infty/K$ is a $\BZ_p$-extension, then for any $n\geq 0$, define $K_n:=K_\infty^{\Gamma^{p^n}}$.

nodes.statement_short: A Galois extension with group $\cong\BZ_p$; $K_n$ is the fixed field of $\Gamma^{p^n}$.

nodes.name: Iwasawa's theorem
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field, $p$ be a prime, $K_\infty/K$ be a $\BZ_p$-extension. Then there exist integers $\lambda\geq 0,\mu\geq 0,\nu$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$, $\ord_p(\#\Cl(K_n))=\mu p^n+\lambda n+\nu$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Iwasawa's theorem on growth of class groups
nodes.statement_short: The $p$-part of the class number of $K_n$ in a $\BZ_p$-extension grows like $\mu p^n+\lambda n+\nu$.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field, $p$ be a prime, $K_\infty/K$ be a $\BZ_p$-extension.
conclusions: there exist integers $\lambda\geq 0,\mu\geq 0,\nu$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$, $\ord_p(\#\Cl(K_n))=\mu p^n+\lambda n+\nu$
nodes.label: clgp-growth

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: For each $n$ let $L_n$ be the maximal unramified abelian extension of $K_n$ of exponent $p$, and let $X_n:=\Gal(L_n/K_n)$. Then by class field theory, $\ord_p(\#\Cl(K_n))=\ord_p(\# X_n)$. Let $L_\infty=\bigcup_n K_n$ and $X_\infty=\Gal(L_\infty/K_\infty)=\varprojlim_n X_n$, then $X_\infty$ is a $\Lambda$-module, where $\Lambda:=\BZ_p[[\Gamma]]$. Theorem \ref{Xn-isom-qout} asserts that $X_\infty$ is a finitely generated torsion $\Lambda$-module and each $X_n$ is isomorphic to certain quotient of $X_\infty$. Proposition \ref{coinvariant-growth-2} asserts the growth of such quotient is of form $\mu p^n+\lambda n+\nu$.

nodes.name: Prime filtration of a finitely generated module
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring and $M$ be a finitely generated $A$-module. Then there exists a chain of submodules of $M$ \[0 = M_0 \subset M_1 \subset \cdots \subset M_n = M\] such that for each $1\leq i\leq n$, $M_i/M_{i-1} \cong A/\fp_i$ for some prime ideal $\fp_i\in\Spec(A)$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring and $M$ be a finitely generated $A$-module.
conclusions: there exists a chain of submodules of $M$ \[0 = M_0 \subset M_1 \subset \cdots \subset M_n = M\] such that for each $1\leq i\leq n$, $M_i/M_{i-1} \cong A/\fp_i$ for some prime ideal $\fp_i\in\Spec(A)$

nodes.name: Krull's Hauptidealsatz
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring. If $\fa=(a_1,\cdots,a_n)$ is an ideal of $A$ generated by $n$ elements, and $\fp$ is a minimal prime over-ideal of $\fa$, then $\height(\fp)\leq n$. (Mathlib: \docs{Ideal.height_le_spanRank_toENat_of_mem_minimal_primes}.) Conversely, if $\fp$ is a prime ideal of $A$ of height $\leq n$, then there exists an ideal $\fa$ of $A$ generated by $n$ elements, such that $\overline\fp$ is a minimal prime in $A/\fa$. (Mathlib: \docs{Ideal.exists_spanRank_eq_and_height_eq}, \docs{Ideal.height_le_iff_exists_minimalPrimes}.)
nodes.statement_short: Minimal primes over an $n$-generated ideal have height $\le n$, and conversely every prime of height $\le n$ is minimal over some $n$-generated ideal.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring.
$\fa=(a_1,\cdots,a_n)$ is an ideal of $A$ generated by $n$ elements
$\fp$ is a minimal prime over-ideal of $\fa$

conclusions: $\height(\fp)\leq n$

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $\fp$ is a minimal prime over-ideal of $\fa$, then $\fa A_\fp\subset\fp A_\fp$, and $\fp(A_\fp/\fa A_\fp)$, which is the only maximal ideal of $A_\fp/\fa A_\fp$, is also a minimal prime ideal. Therefore $A_\fp/\fa A_\fp$ is Artinian, and so $\fa A_\fp$ is an open ideal. It follows that $\height(\fp)=\dim(A_\fp)\leq n$. Conversely, if $\fp$ is a prime ideal of height $\leq n$, then $\dim(A_\fp)\leq n$, so there exists an \emph{ideal of definition} $IA_\fp$ of $A_\fp$ (i.e.~an open ideal with respect to $\fp A_\fp$-adic topology), generated by $n$ elements. Clearing their denominators we may assume that the generators take the form $\frac{x_1}s,\cdots,\frac{x_n}s$ for some $x_1,\cdots,x_n\in I$ and $s\in A\setminus\fp$. Since $\fp^NA_\fp\subset IA_\fp\subset\fp A_\fp$ for some integer $N\geq 1$, we obtain $\fp^N\subset I\subset\fp$, and $IA_\fp=(x_1,\cdots,x_n)A_\fp$ (hence we may replace $I$ by $(x_1,\cdots,x_n)$), and that $\fp$ is a minimal prime over-ideal of $I$ (since if $I\subset\fp'\subset\fp$ for some prime ideal $\fp'$, then $\fp^N\subset\fp'$, hence $\fp\subset\fp'$, so $\fp=\fp'$).
nodes.statement_short: Localize at $\fp$ and use that $A_\fp/\fa A_\fp$ is Artinian; for the converse, clear denominators of a system of parameters of $A_\fp$.

Therefore $A_\fp/\fa A_\fp$ is Artinian, and so $\fa A_\fp$ is an open ideal. It follows that $\height(\fp)=\dim(A_\fp)\leq n$.

nodes.name: UFD criterion via height-one primes
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian domain. Then $A$ is a UFD if and only if every prime ideal of height $1$ is principal (recall that a prime ideal $\fp$ is of height $1$ if $\fp \neq 0$ and there is no prime ideal lies in between $0$ and $\fp$). (We only need ``$\Rightarrow$'' in our project.)
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Noetherian domain.
conclusions: $A$ is a UFD if and only if every prime ideal of height $1$ is principal
equivalent_conditions: every prime ideal of height $1$ is principal
nodes.label: UFD-iff-ht-1-principal

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: ``$\Rightarrow$'': Let $\fp$ be a prime ideal of height $1$, and let $a\in\fp$ be a non-zero element. Factor $a$ into a product of irreducible elements (= prime elements) $a=p_1\cdots p_r$. Then by $a\in\fp$ we obtain $p_i\in\fp$ for some $i$, since $(p_i)\neq 0$ is a prime ideal contained in $\fp$, we have $\fp=(p_i)$. ``$\Leftarrow$'': It suffices to show that every irreducible element is prime. Let $p\in A$ be irreducible, and $\fp$ be a prime ideal of $A$ minimal containing $p$. Then $\fp$ is of height $1$ by Krull's Hauptidealsatz (Theorem \ref{krull-principal-ideal-thm}), so $\fp=(\pi)$ is principal. Since $p\in\fp=(\pi)$, $\pi\mid p$, and since $p$ is irreducible, $p=u\pi$ for some unit $u$, therefore $p$ is prime (which generates $\fp$).
nodes.statement_short: Forward: a prime factor of an element of $\fp$ generates $\fp$. Converse: an irreducible lies in a height-one (by Krull) hence principal prime, so it is prime.

nodes.name: Nakayama lemma, pro-p version
nodes.statement: Suppose $\Lambda\cong\BZ_p[[T]]$, $X$ is a pro-$p$ $\Lambda$-module, $x_1,\cdots,x_t\in X$ such that their images in $X/TX$ generate $X/TX$ as a $\Lambda/(T)$-module. Then $x_1,\cdots,x_t$ generate $X$ as a $\Lambda$-module.
assumptions: Suppose $\Lambda\cong\BZ_p[[T]]$,
$X$ is a pro-$p$ $\Lambda$-module,
$x_1,\cdots,x_t\in X$ such that their images in $X/TX$ generate $X/TX$ as a $\Lambda/(T)$-module.
conclusions: $x_1,\cdots,x_t$ generate $X$ as a $\Lambda$-module
nodes.label: p:nak

nodes.name: Generalizations of the pro-p Nakayama lemma
nodes.statement:
Similar result holds when $T$ is replaced
by a topologically nilpotent element.
Also for several variable formal power series.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $Y:=\Lambda x_1+\cdots+\Lambda x_t$ be the $\Lambda$-submodule of $X$ generated by $x_1,\cdots,x_t$. Then by the image of $Y$ in $X/TX$ is $X/TX$, we know that $Y+TX=X$. Note that $Y$ is compact, so it is closed in $X$, so $Z:=X/Y$ is a pro-$p$ abelian group, and the image of $TX$ in $Z$ is $TZ$. On the other hand, by $Y+TX=X$, the image of $TX$ in $Z$ is also $Z$, so $TZ=Z$. Since $T$ is topologically nilpotent in $\Lambda$, for any open subgroup $U$ of $Z$, there exists $N\geq 0$ such that for any $n\geq N$, $T^nZ\subset U$. But by $TZ=Z$ we know that $T^nZ=Z$ for any $n\geq 0$. Therefore $Z$ must be zero.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to $Z=X/Y$, show $TZ=Z$, and use topological nilpotence of $T$ to force $Z=0$.

nodes.statement_short: Let $Y$ be the span of the $x_i$; then $Y+TX=X$

nodes.name: Define Z
nodes.statement: Note that $Y$ is compact, so it is closed in $X$, so $Z:=X/Y$ is a pro-$p$ abelian group, and the image of $TX$ in $Z$ is $TZ$.
nodes.statement_short: $Y$ is closed so $Z=X/Y$ is pro-$p$

nodes.name: TZ=Z
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by $Y+TX=X$, the image of $TX$ in $Z$ is also $Z$, so $TZ=Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce $TZ=Z$

nodes.name: Topological nilpotence
nodes.statement: Since $T$ is topologically nilpotent in $\Lambda$, for any open subgroup $U$ of $Z$, there exists $N\geq 0$ such that for any $n\geq N$, $T^nZ\subset U$.
nodes.statement_short: Powers of $T$ push $Z$ into any open subgroup

nodes.name: Conclude Z=0
nodes.statement: But by $TZ=Z$ we know that $T^nZ=Z$ for any $n\geq 0$. Therefore $Z$ must be zero.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $Z=0$

nodes.name: Characterizations of DVRs
nodes.statement: For a Noetherian local domain $A$ of dimension one, the following are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item $A$ is integrally closed. \item The maximal ideal of $A$ is principal. \item $A$ is a discrete valuation ring. \item $A$ is a regular local ring. \end{itemize} (Mathlib: \docs{IsDiscreteValuationRing.TFAE} and \docs{tfae_of_isNoetherianRing_of_isLocalRing_of_isDomain}.)
assumptions: a Noetherian local domain $A$ of dimension one
conclusions: the following are equivalent.
equivalent_conditions: The maximal ideal of $A$ is principal.
nodes.label: noeth-local-domain-is-icd-iff

nodes.name: Krull domain
nodes.statement: An integral domain $A$ is called a \emph{Krull domain} if it satisfies the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item $A_\fp$ is a discrete valuation ring for all height one primes $\fp$ of $A$, \item $A=\bigcap_{\fp\in\Spec(A),\height(\fp)=1}A_\fp$ inside $\Frac(A)$, \item any nonzero element of $A$ is contained in only a finitely many height one primes of $A$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Integral closedness is local
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a domain, $S$ be a subset of $\Spec(A)$ such that $A_\fp$ is integrally closed for all $\fp\in S$ and $\bigcap_{\fp\in S}A_\fp=A$ inside $\Frac(A)$. Then $A$ itself is integrally closed. (Mathlib: \docs{IsIntegrallyClosed.of_localization}.)
assumptions: Let $A$ be a domain, $S$ be a subset of $\Spec(A)$ such that $A_\fp$ is integrally closed for all $\fp\in S$ and $\bigcap_{\fp\in S}A_\fp=A$ inside $\Frac(A)$.
conclusions: $A$ itself is integrally closed
nodes.label: integrally-closed-is-local-prop

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Suppose $x\in\Frac(A)$ is integral over $A$. Then it's also integral over $A_\fp$ for all $\fp\in\Spec(A)$. Hence $x\in A_\fp$ for all $\fp\in S$. So $x\in\bigcap_{\fp\in S}A_\fp=A$.
nodes.statement_short: An element integral over $A$ lies in every $A_\fp$, hence in their intersection $A$.

nodes.name: Finite generation over a semilocal ring is local
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a semilocal ring, $M$ be an $A$-module such that for any maximal ideal $\fm$ of $A$, $M_\fm$ is a finitely generated $A_\fm$-module. Then $M$ is a finitely generated $A$-module.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a semilocal ring, $M$ be an $A$-module such that for any maximal ideal $\fm$ of $A$, $M_\fm$ is a finitely generated $A_\fm$-module.
conclusions: $M$ is a finitely generated $A$-module
nodes.label: semilocal-fg-mod

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Suppose $M_{\fm_i}$ is generated by $\{x_{i,1},\cdots, x_{i,n_i}\}$ for each maximal ideal $\fm_i$ of $A$. Let $y_{i,k}$ be a numerator of $x_{i,k}$, which is in $A$. We prove that $\bigcup_{i}\{y_{i,1} \cdots, y_{i,n_i}\}$ is a finite set (Since $A$ is semilocal) of generators of $M$. Let $N$ be the $A$-submodule of $M$ generated by $\bigcup_{i}\{y_{i,1} \cdots, y_{i,n_i}\}$. By local property (\docs{Submodule.eq_top_of_localization_maximal}), it suffices to show that $N_{\fm_{i}} = M_{\fm_{i}}$ for all maximal ideals $\fm_i$ of $A$. It's clear that $N_{\fm_{i}} \subseteq M_{\fm_{i}}$, so we only need to show that $M_{\fm_{i}} \subseteq N_{\fm_{i}}$. In other words, need to prove that $M_{\fm_{i}} \subseteq \operatorname{span}_{A_{\fm_i}} f_i (\bigcup_{i}\{y_{i,1} \cdots, y_{i,n_i}\})$ where $f_i : M \to M_{\fm_i}$ is the localization map. It is enough to show the set of generators of $M_{\fm_{i}}$ is contained in right hand side. Take any $x$ in the set of generators of $M_{\fm_{i}}$. It remains to show that the image of a numerator of $x$ under $f_i$ is in the generators of right hand side by \docs{Submodule.mem_of_numerator_image_mem} and \docs{Submodule.mem_span}. i.e. $f_i(y) \in f_i (\bigcup_{i}\{y_{i,1} \cdots, y_{i,n_i}\})$ for some numerator $y$ of $x$. We take $y$ as some $y_{i,k}$ as above. By definition of $y_{i,k}$, we have $f_i(y_{i,k})$ in right hand side.
nodes.statement_short: Collect numerators of local generators at the finitely many maximal ideals and check equality of the span locally.

nodes.name: Local generators

nodes.statement_short: Take local generators and their numerators $y_{i,k}$

nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $M_{\fm_i}\subseteq N_{\fm_i}$

It is enough to show the set of generators of $M_{\fm_{i}}$ is contained in right hand side.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to generators of $M_{\fm_i}$ lying in the span

nodes.name: Take generator
nodes.statement: Take any $x$ in the set of generators of $M_{\fm_{i}}$. nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a numerator of a generator

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We take $y$ as some $y_{i,k}$ as above. By definition of $y_{i,k}$, we have $f_i(y_{i,k})$ in right hand side.
nodes.statement_short: Take $y=y_{i,k}$, which lies in the span

nodes.name: Semilocal domain with PID localizations is a PID
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a semilocal (i.e.~only finitely many maximal ideals) integral domain, such that for every maximal ideal $\fp$ of $A$, $A_\fp$ is a PID. Then $A$ itself is a PID.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a semilocal (i.e.~only finitely many maximal ideals) integral domain, such that for every maximal ideal $\fp$ of $A$, $A_\fp$ is a PID.
conclusions: $A$ itself is a PID
nodes.label: semilocal-PID

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: It's known that a semilocal Dedeking domain is a PID (\docs{IsPrincipalIdealRing.of_finite_maximals}). So we only need to show $A$ is a Dedekind domain. Let $I$ be any ideal of $A$. Apply Lemma \ref{semilocal-fg-mod} to $I$ we know that $I$ is finitely generated. Hence $A$ is a Noetherian ring. Apply \docs{Ring.krullDimLE_of_isLocalization_maximal}. If $\dim(A_{\fm}) \le n$ for any maximal ideals $\fm$ of $A$, then $\dim(A) \le n$. Hence we have $\dim(A) \le 1$. It's known that if the localizations of a domain at all maximal ideals are integrally closed, then the domain itself is integrally closed (\docs{IsIntegrallyClosed.of_isLocalization_maximal}). Hence our $A$ is integrally closed. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing $A$ is Dedekind: Noetherian by the semilocal finite-generation lemma, dimension $\le1$ and integrally closed by local checks.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It's known that a semilocal Dedeking domain is a PID (\docs{IsPrincipalIdealRing.of_finite_maximals}). So we only need to show $A$ is a Dedekind domain.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $A$ being a Dedekind domain

nodes.name: Noetherian
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be any ideal of $A$. Apply Lemma \ref{semilocal-fg-mod} to $I$ we know that $I$ is finitely generated. Hence $A$ is a Noetherian ring.
nodes.statement_short: Noetherian via Lemma semilocal-fg-mod

nodes.name: Dimension
nodes.statement: Apply \docs{Ring.krullDimLE_of_isLocalization_maximal}. If $\dim(A_{\fm}) \le n$ for any maximal ideals $\fm$ of $A$, then $\dim(A) \le n$. Hence we have $\dim(A) \le 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension at most one by localization

nodes.name: Integrally closed
nodes.statement: It's known that if the localizations of a domain at all maximal ideals are integrally closed, then the domain itself is integrally closed (\docs{IsIntegrallyClosed.of_isLocalization_maximal}). Hence our $A$ is integrally closed. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Integrally closed by localization; done

nodes.name: Characteristic ideal
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, $M$ be a finitely generated torsion $A$-module. The \emph{characteristic ideal} of $M$, denoted by $\chaR_A(M)$, or simply $\chaR(M)$ if there is no risk of confusion, is defined to be $$ \chaR_A(M):=\prod_{\substack{\fp\in\Spec(A)\\ \height(\fp)=1}}\fp^{\ell_{A_\fp}(M_\fp)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\chaR_A(M)$ is the product over height-one primes $\fp$ of $\fp^{\ell(M_\fp)}$.
nodes.label: char-ideal

nodes.name: Multiplicativity of the characteristic ideal
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring. Let $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to 0$ be a short exact sequence of finitely generated $A$-modules. Then $M$ is $A$-torsion if and only if $M'$ and $M''$ are $A$-torsion. If $M$ is $A$-torsion, then $\chaR_A(M)=\chaR_A(M')\chaR_A(M'')$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring.
Let $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to 0$ be a short exact sequence of finitely generated $A$-modules.
If $M$ is $A$-torsion
conclusions: $M$ is $A$-torsion if and only if $M'$ and $M''$ are $A$-torsion.
$\chaR_A(M)=\chaR_A(M')\chaR_A(M'')$
$M$ is $A$-torsion if and only if $M'$ and $M''$ are $A$-torsion.

assumptions: If $M$ is $A$-torsion
conclusions: $\chaR_A(M)=\chaR_A(M')\chaR_A(M'')$

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Since localization is exact, for any prime ideal $\fp$ of $A$, the $0\to M_\fp'\to M_\fp\to M_\fp''\to 0$ is exact. Let $\fp$ runs over all minimal prime ideals of $A$, we obtain that $M$ is $A$-torsion if and only if $M'$ and $M''$ are $A$-torsion. Also, we have $\ell_{A_\fp}(M_\fp)=\ell_{A_\fp}(M_\fp')+\ell_{A_\fp}(M_\fp'')$, hence $\chaR_A(M)=\chaR_A(M')\chaR_A(M'')$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Localization is exact; additivity of length at each height-one prime gives multiplicativity.

nodes.name: Exactness

nodes.statement_short: Minimal primes give the torsion equivalence; additivity of length gives the product formula

nodes.name: Pseudo-null module and pseudo-isomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring. {\rm(i)} A finitely generated $A$-module $M$ is called a \emph{pseudo-null} $A$-module, if $M_\fp=0$ for all prime ideals $\fp$ of $A$ of height $\leq 1$. {\rm(ii)} An $A$-linear homomorphism $f:M\to N$ between finitely generated $A$-modules is called a \emph{pseudo-isomorphism} (\emph{pis} for short), if its kernel and cokernel are pseudo-null $A$-modules. {\rm(iii)} Two finitely generated $A$-modules $M,N$ are called \emph{pseudo-isomorphic} (\emph{pis} for short), denoted by $M\sim_\pis N$ or simply $M\sim N$, if there exists a pseudo-isomorphism from $M$ to $N$.
nodes.statement_short: Pseudo-null: vanishes at primes of height $\le1$; pseudo-isomorphism: map with pseudo-null kernel and cokernel.
nodes.label: pseudo-null

nodes.name: Pseudo-isomorphism is not symmetric
nodes.statement: We warn the reader that $M\sim N$ not necessarily implies $N\sim M$.

nodes.name: Pseudo-null criterion in low dimension
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, $M$ be a finitely generated $A$-module. {\rm(i)} If $A$ is of Krull dimension $\leq 1$, then $M$ is pseudo-null if and only if $M=0$. {\rm(ii)} If $A$ is of Krull dimension $2$, is a local ring with finite residue field, then $M$ is pseudo-null if and only if the cardinality of $M$ is finite.

If $A$ is of Krull dimension $\leq 1$
If $A$ is of Krull dimension $2$, is a local ring with finite residue field
conclusions: $M$ is pseudo-null if and only if $M=0$

nodes.name: Multiplication by a is a pseudo-isomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, $M$ be a finitely generated torsion $A$-module, $a\in A$ such that $M_\fp=0$ for all height one primes of $A$ containing $a$. Then the map $a:M\xrightarrow{\times a}M$ is a pseudo-isomorphism.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, $M$ be a finitely generated torsion $A$-module, $a\in A$ such that $M_\fp=0$ for all height one primes of $A$ containing $a$.
conclusions: the map $a:M\xrightarrow{\times a}M$ is a pseudo-isomorphism
nodes.label: smul-is-pis

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $K$ and $L$ be the kernel and cokernel of the map $a:M\xrightarrow{\times a}M$, respectively. Since localization is exact, for any prime ideal $\fp$ of $A$, the sequence $0\to K_\fp\to M_\fp\xrightarrow{\times a}M_\fp\to L_\fp\to 0$ is exact. If $\fp$ is a minimal prime ideal of $A$, then by $M$ is torsion, we have $M_\fp=0$; if $\fp$ is a height one prime of $A$ such that $a\in\fp$, then by the assumption we know that $M_\fp=0$, hence $K_\fp=L_\fp=0$. If $\fp$ is a height one prime of $A$ such that $a\notin\fp$, then $a$ is invertible in $A_\fp$, hence the map $M_\fp\xrightarrow{\times a}M_\fp$ is an isomorphism, so we also have $K_\fp=L_\fp=0$. Therefore $K$ and $L$ are pseudo-null.
nodes.statement_short: Localize the four-term exact sequence at each prime of height $\le1$ and check kernel and cokernel vanish case by case.

nodes.name: Kernel and cokernel
nodes.statement: Let $K$ and $L$ be the kernel and cokernel of the map $a:M\xrightarrow{\times a}M$, respectively. Since localization is exact, for any prime ideal $\fp$ of $A$, the sequence $0\to K_\fp\to M_\fp\xrightarrow{\times a}M_\fp\to L_\fp\to 0$ is exact.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce kernel and cokernel; localize the exact sequence

nodes.name: Case a in p
nodes.statement: If $\fp$ is a minimal prime ideal of $A$, then by $M$ is torsion, we have $M_\fp=0$; if $\fp$ is a height one prime of $A$ such that $a\in\fp$, then by the assumption we know that $M_\fp=0$, hence $K_\fp=L_\fp=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimal primes and height-one primes containing $a$: $M_\fp=0$

nodes.name: Case a not in p
nodes.statement: If $\fp$ is a height one prime of $A$ such that $a\notin\fp$, then $a$ is invertible in $A_\fp$, hence the map $M_\fp\xrightarrow{\times a}M_\fp$ is an isomorphism, so we also have $K_\fp=L_\fp=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Height-one primes not containing $a$: $a$ is a unit

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $K$ and $L$ are pseudo-null.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel and cokernel are pseudo-null

nodes.name: Height one localizations are PID

nodes.name: Pseudo-isomorphism criterion by semilocalization
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring and let $M,N$ be finitely generated torsion $A$-modules. Let $\Sigma=\{\fq_1,\cdots,\fq_r\} =\{\fq\in\Supp(M)\cup\Supp(N)\mid\height(\fq)=1\}$ (by Proposition \ref{char-ideal-preliminary} this is a finite set). Let $S:=A\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^r\fq_i$ which is a multiplicative subset of $A$. Let $f:M\to N$ be an $A$-module homomorphism. Then $f$ is a pseudo-isomorphism if and only if $S^{-1}f:S^{-1}M\to S^{-1}N$ is an isomorphism.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring and let $M,N$ be finitely generated torsion $A$-modules.
Let $S:=A\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^r\fq_i$ which is a multiplicative subset of $A$.
Let $f:M\to N$ be an $A$-module homomorphism.
conclusions: $f$ is a pseudo-isomorphism if and only if $S^{-1}f:S^{-1}M\to S^{-1}N$ is an isomorphism
nodes.label: pis-iff

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Since the height one support of $\ker(f)$ and $\coker(f)$ are contained in $\Sigma$, and since $S^{-1}\ker(f)=\ker(S^{-1}f)$, $S^{-1}\coker(f)=\coker(S^{-1}f)$ (localization is exact), we only need to prove that if $M$ is a finitely generated torsion $A$-module whose height one support is contained in $\Sigma$, then $S^{-1}M=0$ if and only if $M$ is pseudo-null (equivalently, $M_\fq=0$ for all $\fq\in\Sigma$), which is Lemma \ref{pseudo-null-iff-localization-eq-zero} below.
nodes.statement_short: Localization is exact, so reduce to the pseudo-null criterion for kernel and cokernel.

nodes.name: Pseudo-null iff semilocalization vanishes
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a finitely generated torsion $A$-module, $\Sigma$ be a finite set of height one prime ideals of $A$, containing height one support of $M$. Let $S:=A\setminus\bigcup_{\fq\in\Sigma}\fq$ which is a multiplicative subset of $A$. Then $M$ is pseudo-null if and only if $S^{-1}M=0$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be a finitely generated torsion $A$-module, $\Sigma$ be a finite set of height one prime ideals of $A$, containing height one support of $M$.
Let $S:=A\setminus\bigcup_{\fq\in\Sigma}\fq$ which is a multiplicative subset of $A$.
conclusions: $M$ is pseudo-null if and only if $S^{-1}M=0$
nodes.label: pseudo-null-iff-localization-eq-zero

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: ``$\Leftarrow$'': Clear. ``$\Rightarrow$'': For all $\fq\in\Sigma$, $M_\fq=0$ means that $\Ann(M)\not\subset\fq$, since $\fq$ are prime ideals, we have $\Ann(M)\not\subset\bigcup_{\fq\in\Sigma}\fq$, so $S^{-1}M=0$.
nodes.statement_short: One direction is clear; the other uses prime avoidance on $\Ann(M)$.

nodes.name: Easy direction
nodes.statement: ``$\Leftarrow$'': Clear.
nodes.statement_short: Converse is immediate

nodes.name: Prime avoidance
nodes.statement: ``$\Rightarrow$'': For all $\fq\in\Sigma$, $M_\fq=0$ means that $\Ann(M)\not\subset\fq$, since $\fq$ are prime ideals, we have $\Ann(M)\not\subset\bigcup_{\fq\in\Sigma}\fq$, so $S^{-1}M=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Prime avoidance gives $\Ann(M)\cap S\neq\varnothing$

nodes.name: Structure theorem of finitely generated torsion A-modules
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring whose height one localizations are PID (Definition \ref{ht-1-localization-is-PID}). Let $M$ be a finitely generated torsion $A$-module. Then there exist height one primes $\fp_1,\cdots,\fp_s$ of $A$ and positive integers $k_1,\cdots,k_s$, such that there exists a pseudo-isomorphism $M\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^s A/\fp_i^{k_i}$. Moreover, the sequence $(\fp_i^{k_i})_{i=1}^s$ is unique up to ordering.
nodes.statement_short: A f.g. torsion module is pseudo-isomorphic to a unique sum of $A/\fp_i^{k_i}$ over height-one primes.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring whose height one localizations are PID (Definition \ref{ht-1-localization-is-PID}).
Let $M$ be a finitely generated torsion $A$-module.
conclusions: there exist height one primes $\fp_1,\cdots,\fp_s$ of $A$ and positive integers $k_1,\cdots,k_s$, such that there exists a pseudo-isomorphism $M\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^s A/\fp_i^{k_i}$.
the sequence $(\fp_i^{k_i})_{i=1}^s$ is unique up to ordering
nodes.label: structure-thm

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma=\{\fq_1,\cdots,\fq_r\}=\{\fq\in\Supp(M)\mid\height(\fq)=1\}$ (by Proposition \ref{char-ideal-preliminary} this is a finite set), and let $S=A\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^r\fq_i$. We may assume $\Sigma\neq\varnothing$. Then $S^{-1}M$ is a finitely generated $S^{-1}A$-module, and is torsion (for example, since $\Hom_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M,S^{-1}A) =S^{-1}\Hom_A(M,A)=0$). Note that the prime ideals $\fP$ of $S^{-1}A$ are one-to-one correspondence to prime ideals $\fp$ of $A$ satisfying $\fp\cap S=\varnothing$ (i.e.~$\fp\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^r\fq_i$, i.e~$\fp\subset\fq_i$ for some $i$), by $\fP=S^{-1}\fp$ and $\fp=\fP\cap A$. In particular, $S^{-1}A$ is of dimension $\leq 1$. By structure theorem of finitely generated torsion modules over a PID, there exist primes $\fp_1,\cdots,\fp_s$ of $A$ satisfying $\fp_i\cap S=\varnothing$, and positive integers $k_1,\cdots,k_s$, such that there exists an isomorphism $g:S^{-1}M\xrightarrow\sim\bigoplus_{i=1}^sS^{-1}(A/\fp_i^{k_i})$ of $S^{-1}A$-modules. Since $S^{-1}M$ is torsion, the $\fp_i$'s must be of height one. Since $\Hom_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M,\bigoplus_{i=1}^sS^{-1}(A/\fp_i^{k_i})) =S^{-1}\Hom_A(M,\bigoplus_{i=1}^sA/\fp_i^{k_i})$, by multiplying an element of $S$ to $g$ if necessary (this doesn't change the fact that $g$ is an isomorphism), we may find an $A$-linear map $f:M\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^sA/\fp_i^{k_i}$ such that $g=S^{-1}f$. Now by (i) we know that $f$ is a pseudo-isomorphism. Conversely, if $(\fp_i^{k_i})_{i=1}^s$ is such that there exists a pseudo-isomorphism $M\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^s A/\fp_i^{k_i}$, then enlarging $S$ if necessary, by Lemma \ref{pis-iff}, its localization $S^{-1}M\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^sS^{-1}(A/\fp_i^{k_i})$ is an isomorphism of $S^{-1}A$-module, hence by structure theorem of finitely generated torsion modules over a PID, the $(\fp_i^{k_i})_{i=1}^s$ is unique up to ordering.
nodes.statement_short: Semilocalize at the finitely many height-one primes in the support to get a PID, apply the PID structure theorem, and lift the isomorphism to a pseudo-isomorphism.

nodes.name: Semilocalize
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma=\{\fq_1,\cdots,\fq_r\}=\{\fq\in\Supp(M)\mid\height(\fq)=1\}$ (by Proposition \ref{char-ideal-preliminary} this is a finite set), and let $S=A\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^r\fq_i$. We may assume $\Sigma\neq\varnothing$.

nodes.name: Torsion localization
nodes.statement: Then $S^{-1}M$ is a finitely generated $S^{-1}A$-module, and is torsion (for example, since $\Hom_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M,S^{-1}A) =S^{-1}\Hom_A(M,A)=0$).

In particular, $S^{-1}A$ is of dimension $\leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: $S^{-1}A$ has dimension $\le1$

nodes.name: PID structure theorem
nodes.statement: By structure theorem of finitely generated torsion modules over a PID, there exist primes $\fp_1,\cdots,\fp_s$ of $A$ satisfying $\fp_i\cap S=\varnothing$, and positive integers $k_1,\cdots,k_s$, such that there exists an isomorphism $g:S^{-1}M\xrightarrow\sim\bigoplus_{i=1}^sS^{-1}(A/\fp_i^{k_i})$ of $S^{-1}A$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the PID structure theorem

nodes.name: Height one
nodes.statement: Since $S^{-1}M$ is torsion, the $\fp_i$'s must be of height one.
nodes.statement_short: The primes are of height one

nodes.name: Lift
nodes.statement: Since $\Hom_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M,\bigoplus_{i=1}^sS^{-1}(A/\fp_i^{k_i})) =S^{-1}\Hom_A(M,\bigoplus_{i=1}^sA/\fp_i^{k_i})$, by multiplying an element of $S$ to $g$ if necessary (this doesn't change the fact that $g$ is an isomorphism), we may find an $A$-linear map $f:M\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^sA/\fp_i^{k_i}$ such that $g=S^{-1}f$.

nodes.name: Existence
nodes.statement: Now by (i) we know that $f$ is a pseudo-isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is a pseudo-isomorphism

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $(\fp_i^{k_i})_{i=1}^s$ is such that there exists a pseudo-isomorphism $M\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^s A/\fp_i^{k_i}$, then enlarging $S$ if necessary, by Lemma \ref{pis-iff}, its localization $S^{-1}M\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^sS^{-1}(A/\fp_i^{k_i})$ is an isomorphism of $S^{-1}A$-module, hence by structure theorem of finitely generated torsion modules over a PID, the $(\fp_i^{k_i})_{i=1}^s$ is unique up to ordering.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness via the PID structure theorem after localizing

nodes.name: Pseudo-isomorphism is symmetric for good rings
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring whose height one localizations are PID (Definition \ref{ht-1-localization-is-PID}). Let $M,N$ be finitely generated torsion $A$-modules. Then the followings are equivalent: \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] There exists a pseudo-isomorphism $M\to N$. \item[(b)] For any height one prime $\fp$ of $A$, we have $M_\fp\cong N_\fp$. \end{itemize} In particular, if there exists a pseudo-isomorphism $M\to N$, then there also exists a pseudo-isomorphism $N\to M$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring whose height one localizations are PID (Definition \ref{ht-1-localization-is-PID}).
Let $M,N$ be finitely generated torsion $A$-modules.
conclusions: the followings are equivalent:
if there exists a pseudo-isomorphism $M\to N$, then there also exists a pseudo-isomorphism $N\to M$
equivalent_conditions: For any height one prime $\fp$ of $A$, we have $M_\fp\cong N_\fp$.
nodes.label: pis-symm

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: (a)$\Rightarrow$(b): Clear. (b)$\Rightarrow$(a): Let $\Sigma=\{\fq_1,\cdots,\fq_r\} =\{\fq\in\Supp(M)\cup\Supp(N)\mid\height(\fq)=1\}$ (by Proposition \ref{char-ideal-preliminary} this is a finite set), and let $S=A\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^r\fq_i$. We may assume $\Sigma\neq\varnothing$. Since $M_\fp\cong N_\fp$ for all height one primes $\fp$ of $A$, the $S^{-1}M$ and $S^{-1}N$, being finitely generated torsion modules over a PID $S^{-1}A$, are isomorphic. Say $g:S^{-1}M\xrightarrow\sim S^{-1}N$ is an isomorphism of $S^{-1}A$-modules. Since $\Hom_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M,S^{-1}N)=S^{-1}\Hom_A(M,N)$, by multiplying an element of $S$ to $g$ if necessary (this doesn't change the fact that $g$ is an isomorphism), we may find an $A$-linear map $f:M\to N$ such that $g=S^{-1}f$. Now by Lemma \ref{pis-iff} we know that $f$ is a pseudo-isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Semilocalize to a PID where the modules become isomorphic, then lift the isomorphism.

nodes.statement: (a)$\Rightarrow$(b): Clear.
nodes.statement_short: (a) implies (b) is immediate

nodes.name: (b)=>(a)

Now by Lemma \ref{pis-iff} we know that $f$ is a pseudo-isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: (b) implies (a) via semilocalization

nodes.name: Semilocalize
nodes.statement: (b)$\Rightarrow$(a): Let $\Sigma=\{\fq_1,\cdots,\fq_r\} =\{\fq\in\Supp(M)\cup\Supp(N)\mid\height(\fq)=1\}$ (by Proposition \ref{char-ideal-preliminary} this is a finite set), and let $S=A\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^r\fq_i$. We may assume $\Sigma\neq\varnothing$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\Sigma$, $S$

nodes.name: Isomorphic localizations
nodes.statement: Since $M_\fp\cong N_\fp$ for all height one primes $\fp$ of $A$, the $S^{-1}M$ and $S^{-1}N$, being finitely generated torsion modules over a PID $S^{-1}A$, are isomorphic. Say $g:S^{-1}M\xrightarrow\sim S^{-1}N$ is an isomorphism of $S^{-1}A$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: Localized modules over the PID are isomorphic

nodes.statement: Since $\Hom_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M,S^{-1}N)=S^{-1}\Hom_A(M,N)$, by multiplying an element of $S$ to $g$ if necessary (this doesn't change the fact that $g$ is an isomorphism), we may find an $A$-linear map $f:M\to N$ such that $g=S^{-1}f$.

nodes.statement: Now by Lemma \ref{pis-iff} we know that $f$ is a pseudo-isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is a pseudo-isomorphism

nodes.name: Splitting off torsion up to pseudo-isomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring whose height one localizations are PID (Definition \ref{ht-1-localization-is-PID}). Let $M$ be a finitely generated $A$-module, $T\subset M$ be the torsion submodule. Then there exists a pseudo-isomorphism $M\to T\oplus M/T$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring whose height one localizations are PID (Definition \ref{ht-1-localization-is-PID}).
Let $M$ be a finitely generated $A$-module, $T\subset M$ be the torsion submodule.
conclusions: there exists a pseudo-isomorphism $M\to T\oplus M/T$
nodes.label: pis-torsion-oplus-torsion-free

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma=\{\fq_1,\cdots,\fq_r\}=\{\fq\in\Supp(M)\mid\height(\fq)=1\}$ (by Proposition \ref{char-ideal-preliminary} this is a finite set), and let $S=A\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^r\fq_i$. We may assume $\Sigma\neq\varnothing$. Then $0\to S^{-1}T\to S^{-1}M\to S^{-1}(M/T)\to 0$ is a short exact sequence, $S^{-1}(M/T)$ is a finitely generated torsion-free $S^{-1}A$-module, which is free since $S^{-1}A$ is a PID. Hence we can find $f\in\Hom_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M,S^{-1}T)=S^{-1}\Hom_A(M,T)$ such that $S^{-1}T\hookrightarrow S^{-1}M\xrightarrow{f}S^{-1}T$ is the identity map. We can find $a\in S$ and $g\in\Hom_A(M,T)$ such that $af=g$ and such that $T\hookrightarrow M\xrightarrow{g}T$ is $T\xrightarrow{\times a}T$ which is a pseudo-isomorphism by Proposition \ref{smul-is-pis}. Now we have the following commutative diagram of short exact sequences \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} 0\arrow{r} & T\arrow{r}\arrow{d}{\times a} & M\arrow{r}{\pi}\arrow{d}{(g,\pi)} & M/T\arrow{r}\arrow{d}{\id} & 0 \\ 0\arrow{r} & T\arrow{r} & T\oplus M/T\arrow{r} & M/T\arrow{r} & 0, \end{tikzcd} \end{center} by snake lemma we know that the constructed $M\to T\oplus M/T$ is a pseudo-isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Split the torsion sequence after semilocalizing to a PID, clear denominators, and conclude with the snake lemma.

nodes.name: Semilocalize
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma=\{\fq_1,\cdots,\fq_r\}=\{\fq\in\Supp(M)\mid\height(\fq)=1\}$ (by Proposition \ref{char-ideal-preliminary} this is a finite set), and let $S=A\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^r\fq_i$. We may assume $\Sigma\neq\varnothing$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\Sigma$, $S$

nodes.name: Free quotient
nodes.statement: Then $0\to S^{-1}T\to S^{-1}M\to S^{-1}(M/T)\to 0$ is a short exact sequence, $S^{-1}(M/T)$ is a finitely generated torsion-free $S^{-1}A$-module, which is free since $S^{-1}A$ is a PID.
nodes.statement_short: Localized torsion-free quotient is free

nodes.name: Retraction
nodes.statement: Hence we can find $f\in\Hom_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M,S^{-1}T)=S^{-1}\Hom_A(M,T)$ such that $S^{-1}T\hookrightarrow S^{-1}M\xrightarrow{f}S^{-1}T$ is the identity map.
nodes.statement_short: Find a retraction $f$ onto $S^{-1}T$

nodes.name: Clear denominators
nodes.statement: We can find $a\in S$ and $g\in\Hom_A(M,T)$ such that $af=g$ and such that $T\hookrightarrow M\xrightarrow{g}T$ is $T\xrightarrow{\times a}T$ which is a pseudo-isomorphism by Proposition \ref{smul-is-pis}.
nodes.statement_short: Clear denominators; restriction to $T$ is multiplication by $a$

nodes.name: Snake lemma
nodes.statement: Now we have the following commutative diagram of short exact sequences \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} 0\arrow{r} & T\arrow{r}\arrow{d}{\times a} & M\arrow{r}{\pi}\arrow{d}{(g,\pi)} & M/T\arrow{r}\arrow{d}{\id} & 0 \\ 0\arrow{r} & T\arrow{r} & T\oplus M/T\arrow{r} & M/T\arrow{r} & 0, \end{tikzcd} \end{center} by snake lemma we know that the constructed $M\to T\oplus M/T$ is a pseudo-isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Snake lemma gives the pseudo-isomorphism

nodes.name: Regular domains have PID height one localizations
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian regular domain (more generally, a Noetherian integrally closed domain). Then height one localizations of $A$ are PID (Definition \ref{ht-1-localization-is-PID}).
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Noetherian regular domain (more generally, a Noetherian integrally closed domain).
conclusions: height one localizations of $A$ are PID (Definition \ref{ht-1-localization-is-PID})
nodes.label: regular-domain-is-good

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a Noetherian regular domain (more generally, a Noetherian integrally closed domain), then for each height one prime $\fp$ of $A$, $A_\fp$ is a PID. For any finitely many height one primes $\fp_1,\cdots,\fp_r$ of $A$, let $S:=A\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^r\fp_i$, then $S^{-1}A$ is a semilocal integral domain, whose maximal ideals are $S^{-1}\fp_1,\cdots,S^{-1}\fp_r$, and we have $(S^{-1}A)_{S^{-1}\fp_i}=A_{\fp_i}$, therefore by Lemma \ref{semilocal-PID} we know that $S^{-1}A$ is a PID.
nodes.statement_short: Semilocalization is a semilocal domain whose localizations are DVRs, hence a PID.

nodes.name: Topological generator gamma of Gamma
nodes.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime,
$\Gamma$ be a topological abelian group, isomorphic to $\BZ_p$
as a topological abelian group, and let $\gamma\in\Gamma$ be a topological generator
of $\Gamma$ (i.e.~the subgroup $\{\gamma^n\mid n\in\BZ\}$ is dense in $\Gamma$).

nodes.name: Finite quotients Gamma_n
nodes.statement: For each $n\geq 0$ let $\Gamma_n:=\Gamma/\Gamma^{p^n}$.

nodes.name: Iwasawa algebra
nodes.statement: The \emph{Iwasawa algebra} is defined as the completed group algebra $$ \Lambda:=\BZ_p[[\Gamma]]:=\varprojlim_n\BZ_p[\Gamma_n], $$ where the transition map $\BZ_p[\Gamma_{n+1}]\to \BZ_p[\Gamma_n]$ is induced by the natural projection $\Gamma_{n+1}\to\Gamma_n$. Each $\BZ_p[\Gamma_n]$ is a free $\BZ_p$-module of rank $p^n$, we endow it with the $p$-adic topology, and endow $\Lambda$ with the subspace topology of the product topology of $\prod_{n=0}^\infty\BZ_p[\Gamma_n]$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Lambda$ is the inverse limit of the group rings $\BZ_p[\Gamma_n]$, with the induced topology.
nodes.label: Iwasawa-alg-defn

nodes.name: Linear maps are adically continuous
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a ring, $\fa$ be an ideal of $A$. Let $M,N$ be two $A$-modules, and $\varphi:M\to N$ be an $A$-module homomorphism. Then $\varphi$ is continuous if we endow $M,N$ with $\fa$-adic topology. In particular, if $\varphi$ is an $A$-module isomorphism, then it is a homeomorphism of topological spaces if we endow $M,N$ with $\fa$-adic topology.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $x\in M$ and $y:=\varphi(x)\in N$. Let $U$ be any open neighborhood of $y$ in $N$. Then there exists some $n$ such that $y+\fa^nN\subset U$. Take $V=x+\fa^nM$ then it is an open neighborhood of $x$ in $M$, and we have $\varphi(V)=y+\varphi(\fa^nM)=y+\fa^n\varphi(M)\subset y+\fa^nN\subset U$. Therefore $\varphi$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Direct epsilon-style check: $\varphi(x+\fa^nM)\subset y+\fa^nN$.

nodes.name: Finite-level Iwasawa algebra isomorphism
nodes.statement: For each $n\geq 0$, there is an isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-algebras $$ \BZ_p[\Gamma_n]\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[T]/\big((1+T)^{p^n}-1\big),\qquad \gamma\mapsto 1+T. $$ They are all free $\BZ_p$-modules of finite rank, we endow them with $p$-adic topology. By Proposition \ref{linear-map-is-adic-continuous} we know that it is a homeomorphism of topological spaces.
nodes.statement_short: $\BZ_p[\Gamma_n]\cong\BZ_p[T]/((1+T)^{p^n}-1)$ via $\gamma\mapsto1+T$, a homeomorphism for the $p$-adic topologies.
assumptions: For each $n\geq 0$
conclusions: there is an isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-algebras
it is a homeomorphism of topological spaces
nodes.label: Iwasawa-alg-isom-finite-level

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We have $\Gamma/\Gamma^{p^n}\cong\BZ/p^n\BZ$ as an abelian group, and the image of $\gamma\in\Gamma$ in it is a generator of it. By abuse of notation we still denote the image of $\gamma\in\Gamma$ in it by $\gamma$. Then $\BZ[\Gamma/\Gamma^{p^n}]$ as a $\BZ$-module is free of rank $p^n$ and $\{\gamma^k\}_{0\leq k\leq p^n-1}$ is a basis of it. Now it's easy to see that as a $\BZ_p$-module homomorphism, $\BZ_p[\Gamma/\Gamma^{p^n}]\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[T]/\big((1+T)^{p^n}-1\big)$, $\gamma^k\mapsto(1+T)^k$ is well-defined and is a $\BZ_p$-module isomorphism, and preserves multiplication. Therefore it is an isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the bases $\gamma^k$ and $(1+T)^k$ of the two free $\BZ_p$-modules.

nodes.name: Cyclic quotient
nodes.statement: We have $\Gamma/\Gamma^{p^n}\cong\BZ/p^n\BZ$ as an abelian group, and the image of $\gamma\in\Gamma$ in it is a generator of it. By abuse of notation we still denote the image of $\gamma\in\Gamma$ in it by $\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma_n$ is cyclic of order $p^n$ generated by $\gamma$

nodes.name: Bases
nodes.statement: Then $\BZ[\Gamma/\Gamma^{p^n}]$ as a $\BZ$-module is free of rank $p^n$ and $\{\gamma^k\}_{0\leq k\leq p^n-1}$ is a basis of it. Now it's easy to see that as a $\BZ_p$-module homomorphism, $\BZ_p[\Gamma/\Gamma^{p^n}]\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[T]/\big((1+T)^{p^n}-1\big)$, $\gamma^k\mapsto(1+T)^k$ is well-defined and is a $\BZ_p$-module isomorphism, and preserves multiplication.
nodes.statement_short: Group ring has basis $\gamma^k$; map $\gamma^k\mapsto(1+T)^k$ is a module isomorphism

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore it is an isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude algebra isomorphism

nodes.name: Iwasawa algebra is a power series ring

assumptions: where $\BZ_p[[T]]$ is endowed with $(p,T)$-adic topology
conclusions: There is an isomorphism of topological rings $\BZ_p[[T]]\xrightarrow\sim\Lambda$ sending $1+T$ to $\gamma$,
nodes.label: Iwasawa-alg-isom

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We prove that there is a natural isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-algebras $$ \varprojlim_n\BZ_p[T]/\big((1+T)^{p^n}-1\big) \xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[[T]], $$ and which is a homeomorphism of topological spaces, where the topology of the left hand side is the subspace topology of the product topology of the topology defined in Proposition \ref{Iwasawa-alg-isom-finite-level}, and the topology of the right hand side it the $(p,T)$-adic topology. From which we can obtain the isomorphism of topological rings $\Lambda\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[[T]]$ given by $\gamma\mapsto 1+T$. For simplicity of notation, denote $\varphi_n(T):=(1+T)^{p^n}-1$. Clearly, for each $n\geq 0$ and for all $1\leq i\leq p^n-1$, we have $\binom{p^n}{i}\in p\BZ$, hence $\varphi_n(T)\in T^{p^n}+p\BZ[T]_{\deg\leq p^n-1}\subset(p,T)$, in particular $\varphi_n(T)$ is a distinguished polynomial of degree $p^n$. Moreover, $\varphi_{n+1}(T)=\varphi_n(T)\cdot\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(1+T)^{p^ni}$ with $\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(1+T)^{p^ni}\in(p,T)$, hence $\varphi_n(T)\in(p,T)^{n+1}$ for all $n\geq 0$. It's clear that $\BZ_p[T]_{\deg\leq p^n-1}\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[T]/(\varphi_n(T))$ is an isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-modules, and the Weierstrass division (Proposition \ref{weierstrass-division}) implies that $\BZ_p[T]_{\deg\leq p^n-1}\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n(T))$ is also an isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-modules, therefore the natural ring homomorphism $\BZ_p[T]\hookrightarrow\BZ_p[[T]]$ induces an isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-algebras $\BZ_p[T]/(\varphi_n(T))\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n(T))$ (Corollary \ref{isom-given-by-weierstrass-division}). Since each $\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n(T))$ is a free $\BZ_p$-module of finite rank endowed with the $p$-adic topology, we have $\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n(T))\cong\varprojlim_m\BZ_p[[T]]/(p^m,\varphi_n(T))$, where each $\BZ_p[[T]]/(p^m,\varphi_n(T))$ is endowed with discrete topology. Therefore we have the following isomorphisms of rings as well as topological spaces: \begin{align*} \varprojlim_n\overbrace{\BZ_p[T]/(\varphi_n(T))}^{p\text{-adic topology}} \xrightarrow\sim \varprojlim_n\overbrace{\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n(T))}^{p\text{-adic topology}} &\cong \varprojlim_{m,n}\overbrace{\BZ_p[[T]]/(p^m,\varphi_n(T))}^{\text{discrete topology}} \\ &\stackrel{(*)}\cong \varprojlim_k\overbrace{\BZ_p[[T]]/(p,T)^k}^{\text{discrete topology}} \xrightarrow\sim \overbrace{\BZ_p[[T]]}^{(p,T)\text{-adic topology}}, \end{align*} here $(*)$ holds because $\{(p^m,\varphi_n(T))\}_{m\geq 1,n\geq 1}$ and $\{(p,T)^k\}_{k\geq 1}$ are \emph{cofinal}. In fact, for each $k\geq 1$, and for any $m\geq k$ and $n\geq k$, we have $(p^m,\varphi_n(T))\subset(p,T)^k$; conversely, for each $m\geq 1$ and $n\geq 1$, we have $(p,T)^{p^n}\subset(p,\varphi_n(T))$, and $(p,\varphi_n(T))^m\subset(p^m,\varphi_n(T))$, therefore for any $k\geq p^nm$, we have $(p,T)^k\subset(p,T)^{p^nm}\subset(p,\varphi_n(T))^m\subset(p^m,\varphi_n(T))$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\varprojlim\BZ_p[T]/(\varphi_n)$ with $\BZ_p[[T]]$ via Weierstrass division, and show the ideal systems $(p^m,\varphi_n)$ and $(p,T)^k$ are cofinal.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: We prove that there is a natural isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-algebras $$ \varprojlim_n\BZ_p[T]/\big((1+T)^{p^n}-1\big) \xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[[T]], $$ and which is a homeomorphism of topological spaces, where the topology of the left hand side is the subspace topology of the product topology of the topology defined in Proposition \ref{Iwasawa-alg-isom-finite-level}, and the topology of the right hand side it the $(p,T)$-adic topology. From which we can obtain the isomorphism of topological rings $\Lambda\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[[T]]$ given by $\gamma\mapsto 1+T$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to an isomorphism of inverse limits

nodes.name: Define phi_n
nodes.statement: For simplicity of notation, denote $\varphi_n(T):=(1+T)^{p^n}-1$. Clearly, for each $n\geq 0$ and for all $1\leq i\leq p^n-1$, we have $\binom{p^n}{i}\in p\BZ$, hence $\varphi_n(T)\in T^{p^n}+p\BZ[T]_{\deg\leq p^n-1}\subset(p,T)$, in particular $\varphi_n(T)$ is a distinguished polynomial of degree $p^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\varphi_n$; it is distinguished of degree $p^n$

nodes.name: phi_n in powers
nodes.statement: Moreover, $\varphi_{n+1}(T)=\varphi_n(T)\cdot\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(1+T)^{p^ni}$ with $\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(1+T)^{p^ni}\in(p,T)$, hence $\varphi_n(T)\in(p,T)^{n+1}$ for all $n\geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_n\in(p,T)^{n+1}$

nodes.name: Weierstrass division
nodes.statement: It's clear that $\BZ_p[T]_{\deg\leq p^n-1}\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[T]/(\varphi_n(T))$ is an isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-modules, and the Weierstrass division (Proposition \ref{weierstrass-division}) implies that $\BZ_p[T]_{\deg\leq p^n-1}\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n(T))$ is also an isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-modules, therefore the natural ring homomorphism $\BZ_p[T]\hookrightarrow\BZ_p[[T]]$ induces an isomorphism of $\BZ_p$-algebras $\BZ_p[T]/(\varphi_n(T))\xrightarrow\sim\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n(T))$ (Corollary \ref{isom-given-by-weierstrass-division}).
nodes.statement_short: Weierstrass division gives $\BZ_p[T]/(\varphi_n)\cong\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n)$

nodes.name: p-adic completeness
nodes.statement: Since each $\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n(T))$ is a free $\BZ_p$-module of finite rank endowed with the $p$-adic topology, we have $\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n(T))\cong\varprojlim_m\BZ_p[[T]]/(p^m,\varphi_n(T))$, where each $\BZ_p[[T]]/(p^m,\varphi_n(T))$ is endowed with discrete topology.
nodes.statement_short: Each quotient is the limit of discrete quotients

nodes.name: Chain of isomorphisms
nodes.statement: Therefore we have the following isomorphisms of rings as well as topological spaces: \begin{align*} \varprojlim_n\overbrace{\BZ_p[T]/(\varphi_n(T))}^{p\text{-adic topology}} \xrightarrow\sim \varprojlim_n\overbrace{\BZ_p[[T]]/(\varphi_n(T))}^{p\text{-adic topology}} &\cong \varprojlim_{m,n}\overbrace{\BZ_p[[T]]/(p^m,\varphi_n(T))}^{\text{discrete topology}} \\ &\stackrel{(*)}\cong \varprojlim_k\overbrace{\BZ_p[[T]]/(p,T)^k}^{\text{discrete topology}} \xrightarrow\sim \overbrace{\BZ_p[[T]]}^{(p,T)\text{-adic topology}}, \end{align*} here $(*)$ holds because $\{(p^m,\varphi_n(T))\}_{m\geq 1,n\geq 1}$ and $\{(p,T)^k\}_{k\geq 1}$ are \emph{cofinal}.
nodes.statement_short: Chain of isomorphisms of inverse limits

nodes.name: Cofinality
nodes.statement: In fact, for each $k\geq 1$, and for any $m\geq k$ and $n\geq k$, we have $(p^m,\varphi_n(T))\subset(p,T)^k$; conversely, for each $m\geq 1$ and $n\geq 1$, we have $(p,T)^{p^n}\subset(p,\varphi_n(T))$, and $(p,\varphi_n(T))^m\subset(p^m,\varphi_n(T))$, therefore for any $k\geq p^nm$, we have $(p,T)^k\subset(p,T)^{p^nm}\subset(p,\varphi_n(T))^m\subset(p^m,\varphi_n(T))$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify cofinality of the two ideal systems

nodes.name: Distinguished polynomial
nodes.statement: If $(A,\fm,k)$ is a local ring, then a polynomial $f(X)=\sum_{i=0}^na_iX^i\in A[X]$ is called a \emph{distinguished polynomial} if $a_n=1$ and $a_i\in\fm$ for all $0\leq i\leq n-1$. (Mathlib: \docs{Polynomial.IsDistinguishedAt})
nodes.label: distinguished-polynomial

nodes.name: Units in power series rings
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a ring, and let $f(X)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nX^n\in A[[X]]$ be a formal power series. Then $f(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$ if and only if $a_0\in A^\times$. (Mathlib: \docs{PowerSeries.isUnit_iff_constantCoeff})
assumptions: Let $A$ be a ring, and let $f(X)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nX^n\in A[[X]]$ be a formal power series.
conclusions: $f(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$ if and only if $a_0\in A^\times$
nodes.label: power-series-invertible-iff

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $f(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$, then there exists $g(X)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty b_nX^n\in A[[X]]$ such that $f(X)g(X)=1$, therefore by considering constant term we obtain $a_0b_0=1$, hence $a_0\in A^\times$. Conversely, if $a_0\in A^\times$, by multiplying $a_0^{-1}$ to $f(X)$ if necessary, we may assume that $a_0=1$ and $f(X)=1-Xf_1(X)$ for some $f_1(X)\in A[[X]]$. Since $A[[X]]$ is $(X)$-adically complete and separated, it's easy to see that $1+\sum_{k=0}^\infty X^kf_1(X)^k$ converges $(X)$-adically in $A[[X]]$ and which is the inverse of $f(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare constant terms; conversely invert $1-Xf_1$ by a geometric series.

nodes.name: Necessity
nodes.statement: If $f(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$, then there exists $g(X)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty b_nX^n\in A[[X]]$ such that $f(X)g(X)=1$, therefore by considering constant term we obtain $a_0b_0=1$, hence $a_0\in A^\times$.
nodes.statement_short: A unit has unit constant term

nodes.name: Sufficiency
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $a_0\in A^\times$, by multiplying $a_0^{-1}$ to $f(X)$ if necessary, we may assume that $a_0=1$ and $f(X)=1-Xf_1(X)$ for some $f_1(X)\in A[[X]]$. Since $A[[X]]$ is $(X)$-adically complete and separated, it's easy to see that $1+\sum_{k=0}^\infty X^kf_1(X)^k$ converges $(X)$-adically in $A[[X]]$ and which is the inverse of $f(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Geometric series inverts $1-Xf_1$

nodes.name: Weierstrass division
nodes.statement: Let $(A,\fm,k)$ be a complete local ring, $g(X)=\sum_{i=0}^\infty a_iX^i\in A[[X]]\setminus\fm[[X]]$ be a formal power series such that not all of its coefficients are in $\fm$. Let $n\geq 0$ be the integer such that $a_n\in A\setminus\fm=A^\times$ and $a_i\in\fm$ for all $0\leq i\leq n-1$. Then for any $f\in A[[X]]$, there exists a unique formal power series $q(X)\in A[[X]]$ and a unique polynomial $r(X)\in A[X]$ of degree $\leq n-1$ such that $f=gq+r$.
nodes.statement_short: Division by a power series with unit coefficient in degree $n$ (lower ones in $\fm$) has unique quotient and remainder of degree $<n$.
assumptions: Let $(A,\fm,k)$ be a complete local ring,
$g(X)=\sum_{i=0}^\infty a_iX^i\in A[[X]]\setminus\fm[[X]]$ be a formal power series such that not all of its coefficients are in $\fm$.
Let $n\geq 0$ be the integer such that $a_n\in A\setminus\fm=A^\times$ and $a_i\in\fm$ for all $0\leq i\leq n-1$.
conclusions: for any $f\in A[[X]]$, there exists a unique formal power series $q(X)\in A[[X]]$ and a unique polynomial $r(X)\in A[X]$ of degree $\leq n-1$ such that $f=gq+r$
nodes.label: weierstrass-division

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Write $g(X)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i+X^ng_1(X)$ for some $g_1(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$, and $f(X)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_iX^i+X^nf_1(X)$ for some $f_1(X)\in A[[X]]$. We construct a sequence $(q_k)_{k=1}^\infty$ inductively in $A[[X]]$, such that $f-gq_k\in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}+\fm^k[[X]]$, and such that $q_{k+1}(X)-q_k(X)\in\fm^k[[X]]$. We construct $q_1(X):=f_1(X)g_1(X)^{-1}$. Since $a_i\in\fm$ for all $i\leq n-1$, we have \begin{align*} f(X)-g(X)q_1(X)&=f(X)-\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i\right)q_1(X) -X^nf_1(X) \\ &=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_iX^i-\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i\right)q_1(X) \in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}+\fm[[X]]. \end{align*} Suppose $q_k(X)$ is constructed, then we may write $f(X)-g(X)q_k(X)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i^{(k)}X^i+X^ns_k(X)$ for some $s_k(X)\in\fm^k[[X]]$, and we construct $q_{k+1}(X):=q_k(X)+s_k(X)g_1(X)^{-1}$. Then we have \begin{align*} f(X)-g(X)q_{k+1}(X)&=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i^{(k)}X^i+X^ns_k(X) -\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i\right)s_k(X)g_1(X)^{-1} -X^ns_k(X) \\ &=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i^{(k)}X^i-\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i\right)s_k(X)g_1(X)^{-1} \in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}+\fm^{k+1}[[X]]. \end{align*} Since $A[[X]]$ is complete and separated according to the sequence $\{\fm^k[[X]]\}_{k\geq 1}$ of ideals, there exists a unique limit $q(X)\in A[[X]]$ of the sequence $(q_k)_{k=1}^\infty$, which satisfies $r:=f-gq\in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}$. To prove the uniqueness, suppose $q(X)\in A[[X]]$ and $r(X)\in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}$ such that $gq=r$, then we prove by induction that for any $k\geq 0$ we have $q,r\in\fm^k[[X]]$, which implies that $q=r=0$. When $k=0$ there is nothing to prove. Suppose $q,r\in\fm^k[[X]]$ for some $k\geq 0$. Then we have $(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i)q(X)+X^ng_1(X)q(X)=r(X)$, since $a_i\in\fm$ for all $i\leq n-1$, we obtain $r(X)\in\fm^{k+1}[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}$. Multiply $g_1(X)^{-1}$ to both side, we obtain $(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i)q(X)g_1(X)^{-1}+X^nq(X)=r(X)g_1(X)^{-1}$, therefore $q(X)\in\fm^{k+1}[[X]]$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct the quotient by $\fm$-adic successive approximation and take the limit; uniqueness by induction on the $\fm$-adic order.

nodes.name: Decompose
nodes.statement: Write $g(X)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i+X^ng_1(X)$ for some $g_1(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$, and $f(X)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_iX^i+X^nf_1(X)$ for some $f_1(X)\in A[[X]]$.
nodes.statement_short: Split $g$ and $f$ at degree $n$

nodes.name: Approximation plan
nodes.statement: We construct a sequence $(q_k)_{k=1}^\infty$ inductively in $A[[X]]$, such that $f-gq_k\in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}+\fm^k[[X]]$, and such that $q_{k+1}(X)-q_k(X)\in\fm^k[[X]]$.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: approximate quotients $q_k$

nodes.name: Base step
nodes.statement: We construct $q_1(X):=f_1(X)g_1(X)^{-1}$. Since $a_i\in\fm$ for all $i\leq n-1$, we have \begin{align*} f(X)-g(X)q_1(X)&=f(X)-\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i\right)q_1(X) -X^nf_1(X) \\ &=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_iX^i-\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i\right)q_1(X) \in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}+\fm[[X]]. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Suppose $q_k(X)$ is constructed, then we may write $f(X)-g(X)q_k(X)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i^{(k)}X^i+X^ns_k(X)$ for some $s_k(X)\in\fm^k[[X]]$, and we construct $q_{k+1}(X):=q_k(X)+s_k(X)g_1(X)^{-1}$. Then we have \begin{align*} f(X)-g(X)q_{k+1}(X)&=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i^{(k)}X^i+X^ns_k(X) -\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i\right)s_k(X)g_1(X)^{-1} -X^ns_k(X) \\ &=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i^{(k)}X^i-\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i\right)s_k(X)g_1(X)^{-1} \in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}+\fm^{k+1}[[X]]. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Inductive correction $q_{k+1}=q_k+s_kg_1^{-1}$

nodes.name: Existence
nodes.statement: Since $A[[X]]$ is complete and separated according to the sequence $\{\fm^k[[X]]\}_{k\geq 1}$ of ideals, there exists a unique limit $q(X)\in A[[X]]$ of the sequence $(q_k)_{k=1}^\infty$, which satisfies $r:=f-gq\in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the $\fm$-adic limit $q$

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: To prove the uniqueness, suppose $q(X)\in A[[X]]$ and $r(X)\in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}$ such that $gq=r$, then we prove by induction that for any $k\geq 0$ we have $q,r\in\fm^k[[X]]$, which implies that $q=r=0$. When $k=0$ there is nothing to prove. Suppose $q,r\in\fm^k[[X]]$ for some $k\geq 0$. Then we have $(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i)q(X)+X^ng_1(X)q(X)=r(X)$, since $a_i\in\fm$ for all $i\leq n-1$, we obtain $r(X)\in\fm^{k+1}[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}$. Multiply $g_1(X)^{-1}$ to both side, we obtain $(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i)q(X)g_1(X)^{-1}+X^nq(X)=r(X)g_1(X)^{-1}$, therefore $q(X)\in\fm^{k+1}[[X]]$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness by induction on $k$

nodes.name: Reduce
nodes.statement: To prove the uniqueness, suppose $q(X)\in A[[X]]$ and $r(X)\in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}$ such that $gq=r$, then we prove by induction that for any $k\geq 0$ we have $q,r\in\fm^k[[X]]$, which implies that $q=r=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $gq=r$ forcing $q=r=0$

nodes.name: Base
nodes.statement: When $k=0$ there is nothing to prove.
nodes.statement_short: Base case

nodes.name: Induction
nodes.statement: Suppose $q,r\in\fm^k[[X]]$ for some $k\geq 0$. Then we have $(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i)q(X)+X^ng_1(X)q(X)=r(X)$, since $a_i\in\fm$ for all $i\leq n-1$, we obtain $r(X)\in\fm^{k+1}[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}$. Multiply $g_1(X)^{-1}$ to both side, we obtain $(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_iX^i)q(X)g_1(X)^{-1}+X^nq(X)=r(X)g_1(X)^{-1}$, therefore $q(X)\in\fm^{k+1}[[X]]$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step raises the $\fm$-adic order

nodes.name: Polynomial and power series quotients by a distinguished polynomial agree
nodes.statement: Let $(A,\fm,k)$ be a complete local ring, $g(X)=\sum_{i=0}^n a_iX^i\in A[X]$ be a polynomial such that $a_n\in A\setminus\fm$ and $a_i\in\fm$ for all $i<n$. Then the natural map $A[X]/(g)\to A[[X]]/(g)$ is an isomorphism.
assumptions: Let $(A,\fm,k)$ be a complete local ring, $g(X)=\sum_{i=0}^n a_iX^i\in A[X]$ be a polynomial such that $a_n\in A\setminus\fm$ and $a_i\in\fm$ for all $i<n$.
conclusions: the natural map $A[X]/(g)\to A[[X]]/(g)$ is an isomorphism

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $f\in A[[X]]$. Then by Proposition \ref{weierstrass-division}, we may find a unique formal power series $q(X)\in A[[X]]$ and a unique polynomial $r(X)\in A[X]$ of degree $\leq n-1$ such that $f=gq+r$. Then $r$ is the unique inverse of $f$ under the natural map $A[X]/(g)\to A[[X]]/(g)$.
nodes.statement_short: Weierstrass division gives a unique polynomial remainder, the inverse image.

nodes.name: Divide
nodes.statement: Let $f\in A[[X]]$. Then by Proposition \ref{weierstrass-division}, we may find a unique formal power series $q(X)\in A[[X]]$ and a unique polynomial $r(X)\in A[X]$ of degree $\leq n-1$ such that $f=gq+r$.

nodes.statement: Then $r$ is the unique inverse of $f$ under the natural map $A[X]/(g)\to A[[X]]/(g)$.
nodes.statement_short: The remainder is the unique preimage

nodes.name: Weierstrass preparation theorem
nodes.statement: Let $(A,\fm,k)$ be a complete local ring. Let $g(X)\in A[[X]]\setminus\fm[[X]]$ be a formal power series such that not all of its coefficients are in $\fm$. Then there is a unique distinguished polynomial $f(X)\in A[X]$ and a unique invertible formal power series $h(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$ such that $g=fh$.
assumptions: Let $(A,\fm,k)$ be a complete local ring.
Let $g(X)\in A[[X]]\setminus\fm[[X]]$ be a formal power series such that not all of its coefficients are in $\fm$.
conclusions: there is a unique distinguished polynomial $f(X)\in A[X]$ and a unique invertible formal power series $h(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$ such that $g=fh$
nodes.label: weierstrass-preparation

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Take $f(X)=X^n$ in Proposition \ref{weierstrass-division}, we obtain $q(X)\in A[[X]]$ and $r(X)\in A[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}$ such that $X^n=g(X)q(X)+r(X)$. Since $g(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}a_iX^i+X^ng_1(X)$ with $a_i\in\fm$ for all $i\leq n-1$ and $g_1(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$, we have $r(X)\in\fm[X]_{\deg\leq n-1}$, and by the construction in (ii) we have $q(X)\in g_1(X)^{-1}+\fm[[X]]\subset A[[X]]^\times$. Therefore take $h(X):=q(X)^{-1}\in A[[X]]^\times$ and $f(X):=X^n-r(X)$, then $f(X)$ is a distinguished polynomial of degree $n$, and $g(X)=f(X)h(X)$ holds. To prove the uniqueness, suppose $f(X)$ and $f'(X)$ are two distinguished polynomials and $u(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$ such that $f'(X)=f(X)u(X)$. Then $\overline u(X)\in k[[X]]^\times$ and we have $\overline f{}'(X)=X^{\deg(f')}=\overline f(X)\overline u(X) =X^{\deg(f)}\overline u(X)\in k[[X]]^\times$, which forces that $\deg(f)=\deg(f')$ and $\overline u(X)=1$. Therefore $f'(X)-f(X)\in A[X]_{\deg\leq\deg(f)-1}$ and $f'(X)=f(X)+(f'(X)-f(X))$ is a Weierstrass division of $f'$ by $f$, on the other hand, $f'(X)=f(X)u(X)$ is also a Weierstrass division of $f'$ by $f$, hence by the uniqueness of Weierstrass division we have $u(X)=1$ and $f'(X)=f(X)$. (\emph{Another proof.} It is possible to prove Weierstrass preparation theorem using a form of Hensel's lemma presented in \url{https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hensel's+lemma}.)
nodes.statement_short: Divide $X^n$ by $g$ (Weierstrass division) to get $g=(X^n-r)q^{-1}$; uniqueness by reducing mod $\fm$ and uniqueness of division.

nodes.statement_short: Remainder lies in $\fm[X]$ and $q$ is a unit

nodes.name: Factorization
nodes.statement: Therefore take $h(X):=q(X)^{-1}\in A[[X]]^\times$ and $f(X):=X^n-r(X)$, then $f(X)$ is a distinguished polynomial of degree $n$, and $g(X)=f(X)h(X)$ holds.

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: To prove the uniqueness, suppose $f(X)$ and $f'(X)$ are two distinguished polynomials and $u(X)\in A[[X]]^\times$ such that $f'(X)=f(X)u(X)$. Then $\overline u(X)\in k[[X]]^\times$ and we have $\overline f{}'(X)=X^{\deg(f')}=\overline f(X)\overline u(X) =X^{\deg(f)}\overline u(X)\in k[[X]]^\times$, which forces that $\deg(f)=\deg(f')$ and $\overline u(X)=1$. nodes.name: Structure of finitely generated torsion Lambda-modules
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a finitely generated torsion $\Lambda$-module, then there exists a pseudo-isomorphism $$ X\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\Lambda/(f_i^{b_i})\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^s\Lambda/(p^{n_j}) $$ where $f_1,\cdots,f_m$ are irreducible distinguished polynomials. nodes.name: Primes not above p are unramified
nodes.statement: If $K$ is any number field, $K_\infty/K$ is any $\BZ_p$-extension, and $\fl$ is a prime of $K$ not above $p$ (in particular, an infinite place). Then $\fl$ is unramified in $K_\infty/K$.
assumptions: If $K$ is any number field, $K_\infty/K$ is any $\BZ_p$-extension, and $\fl$ is a prime of $K$ not above $p$ (in particular, an infinite place).
conclusions: $\fl$ is unramified in $K_\infty/K$
nodes.label: p:unr-outside-p

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $D_\fl$ be the decomposition subgroup of $\fl$ in $\Gamma:=\Gal(K_\infty/K)\cong\BZ_p$, which is a closed subgroup. If $\fl$ is an infinite place then $D_\fl$ is finite, hence must be trivial. In the following assume $\fl$ is a finite place. Let $l=\chaR(\CO_K/\fl)\neq p$, then $K_\fl/\BQ_l$ is a finite extension, and let $(K_\infty)_\fl:=\varinjlim(K_n)_\fl$, then $D_\fl=\Gal((K_\infty)_\fl/K_\fl)$ is a subgroup of $\BZ_p$. We have $K_\fl\subset K_\fl^{\mathrm{unr}}\subset K_\fl^{\mathrm{ab}}$, and $$ \Gal(K_\fl^{\mathrm{unr}}/K_\fl)\cong\widehat\BZ =\prod_{q\text{ prime}}\BZ_q. $$ So $K_\fl$ has at least one $\BZ_p$-extension, i.e. the unique unramified $\BZ_p$-extension. If there are other $\BZ_p$-extensions of $K_\fl$, then there exists a Galois extension of $K_\fl$ with Galois group isomorphic to $\BZ_p^2$. However, $\Gal(K_\fl^{\mathrm{ab}}/K_\fl^{\mathrm{unr}})$ doesn't have a quotient isomorphic to $\BZ_p$, because by local class field theory, $\Gal(K_\fl^{\mathrm{ab}}/K_\fl^{\mathrm{unr}})\cong\CO_{K_\fl}^\times\cong (\text{a finite group})\times\BZ_l^{[K_\fl:\BQ_l]}$ which is a finite group times a pro-$l$ group, obviously it doesn't have a quotient isomorphic to $\BZ_p$. So there is only one $\BZ_p$-extension of $K_\fl$, note that $(K_\infty)_\fl/K_\fl$ is either trivial or a $\BZ_p$-extension, in both cases it must be contained in $K_\fl^{\mathrm{unr}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Local analysis: a $\BZ_p$-extension of $K_\fl$ ($\ell\neq p$) must be the unramified one, since by local class field theory the inertia part has no $\BZ_p$ quotient.

nodes.name: Totally ramified Z_p-extension
nodes.statement: A $\BZ_p$-extension $K_\infty/K$ is called totally ramified, if all primes which are ramified in $K_\infty/K$ are totally ramified. More explicitly, for any prime of $K$, either it is unramified in $K_n/K$ for all $n$, or it is totally ramified in $K_n/K$ for all $n$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The $Y\subset X_\infty$ is constructed as follows. Let $\fp_1,\cdots,\fp_s$ be primes of $\CO_K$ which are (totally) ramified in $K_\infty$ (they are all above $\fp$ by Lemma \ref{p:unr-outside-p}). For each $\fp_i$ fix a place of $L_\infty$ above it and let $I_i\subset G$ be its inertia subgroup. Since $L_\infty/K_\infty$ is unramified and $K_\infty/K$ is totally ramified at $\fp_i$, we have $I_i\cap X_\infty=1$, and $I_i\hookrightarrow G/X_\infty=\Gamma$ is surjective, hence bijective. Therefore $G=I_iX_\infty=X_\infty I_i$. For each $i$ let $\sigma_i\in I_i$ be the preimage of $\gamma\in\Gamma$, then $\sigma_i$ is a topological generator of $I_i$. For $i=2,\cdots,s$, let $a_i\in X_\infty$ be some element such that $\sigma_i=a_i\sigma_1\in X_\infty I_1=G$. Take $Y$ to be the closure of the $\Lambda$-submodule generated by $a_2,\cdots,a_s$ and $\{(\gamma\bullet x)x^{-1}\mid x\in X_\infty\}$. ... ...
nodes.statement_short: Construct $Y$ from inertia groups of the ramified primes and the commutator-type elements $(\gamma\bullet x)x^{-1}$ (remainder unfinished).
